title: The misery of being human (I.22)
hook: every life has sorrow; the wise make peace with it
tomorrow: what would change if tonight were the last time?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a quiet room that grows sweet if it's kept for God, and the open door beside it, for those who go out to serve. The line was the cell grows sweet.

Scroll long enough and everyone else seems fine. The beach trip, the new car, the couple laughing at a dinner that looks warm through the screen. The Imitation had a version of this, long before screens. Some people, it says, look at someone else and sigh: see how well that person lives, how rich, how great, how powerful. Then it answers with a question. Who has everything just as they want it? Not me, not you, not anyone on earth. Not even, it adds, a king or a pope.
screen: `EVERYONE ELSE SEEMS FINE.` → `SEE HOW WELL THAT PERSON LIVES.` → `NOT EVEN A KING OR A POPE.`

segments.voice: Chapter twenty-two of book one has a title that sounds bleak: the misery of being human. It isn't there to darken anyone's day. It's clearing away a false hope, that somebody, somewhere, has a life without sorrow. Nobody does. And notice where it looks for proof. Not in disasters, or in some tragic story. In the body. Eating, drinking, sleeping, waking, working, resting: the plain needs of a body, which the chapter says a devout person feels as a weight. Hunger at eleven. The yawn at three in the afternoon. The knee that aches when it rains. That's the misery the book means, and everyone with a body shares it. Then it borrows a psalm's prayer. In the Douay-Rheims: "deliver me from my necessities." Then comes the turn, and it's a sharp one. The chapter asks who is actually better off, and it doesn't say the rich one or the healthy one. It says the one who is able to suffer something for God. Having plenty of passing things isn't what makes a person happy, it says; a modest amount is enough. So the envy at the screen loses its footing. The person who looks fine gets hungry at eleven too. Peace doesn't come from finding the life without limits. It comes from turning to God inside the limits everyone shares.
screen: `A FALSE HOPE, CLEARED AWAY.` · `EAT, SLEEP, WAKE, WORK, REST.` · `DELIVER ME FROM MY NECESSITIES.` · `WHO IS BETTER OFF?` · then, large: `EVERYONE HAS SORROW.`

segments.voice: Sit and press both feet into the floor. Notice one thing your body needs right now, water, rest, food, a stretch, and don't fix it yet; just feel it as a limit everyone carries, the famous and the unknown alike. If you pray, you can borrow the psalm: deliver me from my necessities.
The misery of being human. The Imitation's honest line: every life carries trouble, even the one that looks perfect from outside.

howItsDone: Catholics speak of 'offering up' sufferings and accepting limits as part of following Christ, and the Imitation's chapters on human misery are read in spiritual reading and on retreats.

chat.meaning: The Imitation says no one, not even a king or a pope, has everything as they wish. Everyone carries sorrow, often unseen.

pope.meaning: the bishop of Rome, head of the Catholic Church

psalm.meaning: a sacred song from the Bible's book of Psalms

Douay-Rheims.meaning: an older English Catholic translation of the Bible

notes: Imitation I.22 paraphrased: thou art miserable wherever thou art unless thou turn to God; who has all things as he wishes, neither I nor thou nor any man on earth; none without some tribulation, though king or pope; who is better off, he who can suffer something for God; the weak say, see how good a life that man has, how rich, how great, how mighty; it is not man's happiness to have temporal goods in abundance, a mediocrity suffices; to eat, drink, watch, sleep, rest, labor and be subject to the necessities of nature is misery to the devout; 'from my necessities deliver me, O Lord'. Confirm.
